slides.title: Modus ponens
slides.text:
Modus ponens
From an if-then statement and its if-part,
infer its then-part.
The form
An example
If A, then B
If the door is open, you can come in.
The door is open.
A
You can come in.
B
Valid for any statements A and B.
The rule does not look inside A and B, so their reading is everything.

slides.title: When "if" says more
slides.text:
When "if" says more
Unambiguous now: "red spots and red gills".
It still says nothing about other mushrooms.
If you behave well, I will buy you an ice-cream.
The child also hears: behave badly, no ice-cream.
An expectation, not a valid inference.
Formalizing forces the choice. It does not make it for us.
